response.text:
That on Wenlock Edge a young American, seeking only frivolous amusement, should find a legitimate parentage as modern as though just caught in the Severn below, astonished him as much as though he had found Darwin himself. To an American in search of a father, it mattered nothing whether the father breathed through lungs, or walked on fins, or on feet; yet that *Pteraspis* and shark should be older than evolution itself perplexed him. The vertebrate began in the Ludlow shale, as complete as Adams himself, at the top of the column of organic evolution; and geology offered no proof he had ever been anything else. Adams could see in Sir Charles's theory only pure inference, precisely like the inference of Paley that, if one found a watch, one inferred a maker. All he could prove was change.

Behind the lesson of the day, he was conscious that, in geology as in theology, he could prove only Evolution that did not evolve; Uniformity that was not uniform; and Selection that did not select. To other Darwinians—except Darwin—Natural Selection seemed a dogma to be put in the place of the Athanasian creed; a form of religious hope. Adams sympathized warmly, but felt he had no Faith; whenever the next new hobby should be brought out, he should drop off from Darwinism like a monkey from a perch. What he valued most was Motion; what attracted his mind was Change. Henry Adams was the first in an infinite series of ancestors to admit that he did not really care whether truth was, or was not, true. He was a Darwinian for fun.

He put psychology under lock and key, and insisted on aiming at ultimate Unity. For young men whose lives were cast between 1867 and 1900, Law should be Evolution from lower to higher, concentration of multiplicity in unity, compulsion of anarchy in order; and he would force himself to follow wherever it led, though he should sacrifice five thousand millions more in money, and a million more lives.

Quite serious, he attacked the burning question of specie payments, and waded through the British suspension of 1797–1821, learning to his confusion that the Bank of England itself held restriction had been a fatal mistake, and that the best treatment of a debased currency was to let it alone. The shock to his financial principles was more serious than the shock of *Pteraspis* to his geology. He sent two long articles to the *North American*; the editor accepted both. Henceforward he had the freedom of the press.

The last year in England was the pleasantest. He was already old in society, and belonged to the Silurian horizon. The conduct of England during the American Civil War was the last thing London liked to recall, and for the first time the American felt himself almost as strong as an Englishman. His old education was finished; his new one was not begun; he loitered a year, near the end of a long, tempestuous, successful voyage, with another to follow, and a summer sea between.

In February, 1868, he was back in Rome, sitting on the steps of Ara Cœli as had become almost a superstition. The long ten years of accidental education had changed nothing for him there. London had become his vice; he loved his haunts, his houses, his habits, and even his hansom cabs. When at last he found himself back at Liverpool, he had no more acquired education than when he first trod the steps of the Adelphi Hotel in 1858. He took England no longer with the awe of American youth, but with the habit of an old and rather worn suit of clothes.
